prompt: What is the difference between AgentKit and the Agents SDK?

choices.text: AgentKit is the old name of the Agents SDK, kept for backward compatibility
choices.why: They are different kinds of thing that exist side by side.

choices.text: AgentKit is hosted products; the SDK is a library
choices.why: Right. The builder, ChatKit and the registry run on OpenAI's platform; the SDK runs in your process.

choices.text: The SDK is for Python and AgentKit is the same library rewritten for JavaScript
choices.why: Language is not the distinction; one of them is not a library at all.

choices.text: There is none
choices.why: One runs on a vendor's servers, the other in your program.

prompt: Why does the lesson tell you to read OpenAI's current documentation before relying on its table of AgentKit's pieces?

choices.text: Because the table was copied from a competitor's product page
choices.why: It describes OpenAI's own launch.

choices.text: Because hosted products change on the platform's schedule, and none of them could be run here
choices.why: Right. Names, betas and availability move, and this course could not check them.

choices.text: Because the table describes the Agents SDK, which changes weekly
choices.why: The table is about the hosted products, not the library.

choices.text: Because AgentKit was withdrawn
choices.why: The lesson does not say so; it says it could not check.

prompt: oa_run.py talks to Ollama with nothing in it about Ollama. What makes that work?

choices.text: A plugin of the SDK that translates OpenAI's requests for Ollama
choices.why: No plugin is installed; the SDK sends the same requests it would send to OpenAI.

choices.text: Ollama answers the Responses API, and OPENAI_BASE_URL points the SDK at it
choices.why: Right. The SDK's default API is one Ollama speaks, and the address comes from the environment.

choices.text: set_tracing_disabled(True), which switches the SDK to local mode
choices.why: It only stops traces being sent to OpenAI.

choices.text: The model name, which the SDK recognises as a local one
choices.why: The SDK passes the name through; Ollama is what knows llama3.2:3b.

prompt: Match each piece of lesson 7's minagent to its name in the Agents SDK.
The tool result the SDK sent back began `{'id': 'M-1043', ... 'delivered_on': None`. Why does it look like that?

choices.text: The recorder rewrote the JSON into Python before logging it
choices.why: The recorder writes requests as they arrived.

choices.text: Because the Responses API requires tool results in Python syntax
choices.why: Tool results are strings; the API does not care what syntax they use.

choices.text: Because get_order returns a Python string
choices.why: It returns a dict; the SDK turned it into text.

choices.text: The SDK turned the returned dict into text with str()
choices.why: Right. Return a json.dumps string if what the model reads matters.

prompt: The tool definition carried `"strict": true`, and the call for "1044" was still refused by the SDK's own validation. What does that show?

choices.text: The flag asks the provider to constrain arguments; the host still has to check them
choices.why: Right. Whether a provider honours strict mode is the provider's business, so validation stays in the host.

choices.text: Strict mode only applies to numbers, not to string patterns
choices.why: The flag is about the whole schema, not one type.

choices.text: set_tracing_disabled switched strict mode off
choices.why: Tracing and strict mode are unrelated.

choices.text: Strict mode is ignored by every provider
choices.why: It is a real feature of some providers; this request cannot show whether Ollama applies it.

prompt: What does the SDK do when a run reaches max_turns?

choices.text: Returns the last tool result as the final answer
choices.why: No answer is invented; the run ends with an exception.

choices.text: Asks the model to summarise what it has so far
choices.why: Nothing extra is requested; the limit stops the run.

choices.text: Raises MaxTurnsExceeded
choices.why: Right. The program decides what the customer sees, so every run needs that handling.

choices.text: Doubles the limit and continues
choices.why: Limits belong to the host, and the SDK does not raise them.

prompt: With the default settings, what did the model read when get_order failed for M-9999?

choices.text: LookupError: no order M-9999
choices.why: That is what it read after failure_error_function was set.

choices.text: The full Python traceback, file paths included
choices.why: The SDK does not send tracebacks.

choices.text: A generic sentence asking it to try again
choices.why: Right. 'An error occurred while running the tool. Please try again.', the same for every failure.

choices.text: Nothing: the run crashed
choices.why: The run continued; the model answered.

prompt: The function_tool argument that decides what the model reads when a tool raises is `___`.
What name did the SDK give the handoff tool for the agent called 'Orders specialist'?

choices.text: transfer_to_orders_specialist
choices.why: Right. The SDK builds it from the agent's name.

choices.text: handoff_orders
choices.why: The SDK's convention is transfer_to_ plus the name.

choices.text: ask_orders
choices.why: That is the name given to the agent-as-tool, by the program.

choices.text: orders_specialist
choices.why: The SDK prefixes it with transfer_to_.

prompt: In the handoff run, what did the orders specialist receive besides the customer's message?

choices.text: Nothing else: handoffs pass only the customer's words
choices.why: The printed messages show more: the handoff call and its result.

choices.text: The triage agent's system prompt
choices.why: The specialist's system message is its own instructions.

choices.text: The triage agent's handoff call and its result
choices.why: Right. The SDK passes the conversation so far by default; an input_filter changes that.

choices.text: A summary written by the triage agent
choices.why: No summary was written; the conversation itself was passed.

prompt: In the agent-as-tool run, why do all the items belong to the front desk?

choices.text: Because the specialist failed and the front desk answered alone
choices.why: The specialist answered; its answer is the tool's output.

choices.text: Because the SDK merges both agents' histories into one list for convenience
choices.why: The specialist's own steps stayed inside the tool call.

choices.text: Because as_tool copies the specialist's tools into the front desk
choices.why: The front desk has one tool, ask_orders.

choices.text: The specialist ran inside one tool call
choices.why: Right. Its steps are not in the front desk's history, which is lesson 6's boundary.

prompt: What does a run return when the model asks for a tool declared with needs_approval=True?

choices.text: An interruption: the pending call, waiting for a decision
choices.why: Right. result.interruptions holds it, with the tool and its arguments.

choices.text: An error result telling the model it is not allowed
choices.why: That is lesson 7's behaviour with no confirm callback, not the SDK's.

choices.text: The final answer, with the refund already done and logged for review
choices.why: The refund does not run until someone approves it.

choices.text: An exception
choices.why: No exception: the run pauses and returns.

prompt: What can result.to_state() do that lesson 7's confirm callback cannot?

choices.text: Approve refunds automatically below a threshold set in the code
choices.why: Nothing in to_state approves anything; a person or code calls approve.

choices.text: Validate the refund's arguments against the schema
choices.why: Validation happens either way; it is not what the state adds.

choices.text: Be saved and resumed later, after a person answers in a queue
choices.why: Right. The pause outlives the process; the callback has to answer inside the loop.

choices.text: Undo a refund
choices.why: Undoing needs another transaction; the state only pauses before acting.

prompt: After the approved run, how many cents had been refunded on M-1047?
Both guardrail runs refused the message. What did the grep counts show?

choices.text: That neither run sent the card number anywhere
choices.why: The parallel run's count was 1.

choices.text: That both runs sent it, because guardrails always run after the request
choices.why: The blocking run's count was 0.

choices.text: That the blocking run sent it twice
choices.why: It sent nothing.

choices.text: Only the parallel run let it reach the provider
choices.why: Right. The request left before the guardrail tripped: 1 against 0.

prompt: When is the SDK's default, run_in_parallel=True, the right choice for a guardrail?

choices.text: When the guardrail must keep sensitive data from reaching the provider
choices.why: That is exactly when it is wrong: the request may leave first.

choices.text: When its job is to stop a bad answer, and latency matters
choices.why: Right. It costs nothing when it passes, and can still cancel the run before an answer is used.

choices.text: Never, since parallel guardrails cannot trip
choices.why: The parallel one tripped in this lesson's run, after the request had left.

choices.text: Always, since blocking guardrails cost tokens
choices.why: A code guardrail costs no tokens; blocking costs latency.

prompt: Without a session, why did the second message get 'Which order do you mean?'

choices.text: It began from nothing but that turn's own text
choices.why: Right. Nothing of the first turn was sent, so no order was named.

choices.text: Because the SDK deletes the database after each run
choices.why: There was no database in that run at all.

choices.text: Because get_order failed for M-1042 on the second run
choices.why: No get_order call was made in the second run.

choices.text: Because the provider forgot the first turn
choices.why: Providers keep nothing between requests either way; the session is what resends it.

prompt: Why does the lesson say sessions.db belongs in the same inventory as the trace?

choices.text: Because the SDK writes traces into sessions.db
choices.why: They are separate; the point is what both contain.

choices.text: Because both make the agent faster
choices.why: Neither is about speed.

choices.text: It stores customers' messages: personal data the erase path must reach
choices.why: Right. A store of personal data that deletion cannot reach is a defect.

choices.text: Because both are JSON
choices.why: sessions.db is SQLite; the format is beside the point.

prompt: Why does oa_trace.py call set_trace_processors rather than add_trace_processor?

choices.text: Because add_trace_processor only works with the Responses API
choices.why: The choice is about the default exporter, not the API.

choices.text: Because set_trace_processors is faster
choices.why: Speed is not the reason.

choices.text: Because add would keep the exporter that sends spans to OpenAI
choices.why: Right. set replaces the default processors; add puts one beside them.

choices.text: Because add_trace_processor is deprecated
choices.why: The lesson does not say so; the difference is replacing versus adding.
